description: A composite, three-image figure built entirely from XRD line-profile analysis of austenite in two samples (RD and TD). The two upper images are modified Williamson-Hall plots with identical axes: y = ΔK−βW_hkl (nm⁻¹), 0.00–0.10 in 0.02 steps; x = KC^1/2 (nm⁻¹), 1.5–5.0. The left plot is for ε=0.14 and prints β_RD=0.002 and β_TD=0.004 as text; the right plot is for ε=0.22 and prints β_RD=0.0018 and β_TD=0.0044. Red (RD) and blue (TD) fitted lines join five data points labelled with the FCC reflections 111, 200, 220, 311, 222 (filled squares for RD and open squares for TD at ε=0.14; filled and open circles at ε=0.22). At ε=0.14 the red and blue lines nearly coincide, whereas at ε=0.22 the red RD line lies clearly above the blue TD line across the whole range, i.e. the steeper slope tied to higher dislocation density. Panel (b) is a scatter plot of austenite dislocation density (×10^14 m⁻², ticks 0–10) versus true strain (ticks 0.0–0.5): both curves rise monotonically from below 1, the RD curve stays above TD above ~0.05 strain, and the gap narrows at the highest strains.
measured_quantities: true strain levels ε=0.14 and ε=0.22

observations.observation: Both (a) panels use the axes ΔK−βW_hkl (nm⁻¹) from 0.00 to 0.10 on the ordinate and KC^1/2 (nm⁻¹) from 1.5 to 5.0 on the abscissa.
The left (a) panel is labelled ε=0.14 and prints β_RD=0.002, β_TD=0.004; the right (a) panel is labelled ε=0.22 and prints β_RD=0.0018, β_TD=0.0044.
Data points in both (a) panels are annotated with the five FCC reflections 111, 200, 220, 311 and 222, red labels for RD and blue labels for TD.

At ε=0.14 the red (RD) and blue (TD) fitted lines in panel (a) lie almost on top of each other, with the RD points marginally above TD at low KC^1/2 and the two 222 points nearly coincident near KC^1/2≈4.9.
At ε=0.22 the red RD line in panel (a) lies clearly above the blue TD line over the entire KC^1/2 range, i.e. the RD slope is visibly steeper than the TD slope.

Panel (b) plots dislocation density in units of ×10^14 m⁻² (ordinate ticks 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) against true strain (abscissa ticks 0.0 to 0.5 in steps of 0.1) for both the RD (red open circles) and TD (blue open circles) samples.

In panel (b) the austenite dislocation density increases monotonically with true strain for both samples, and the RD curve stays above the TD curve over essentially the whole strain range after the two curves cross at very low strain.
In panel (b) the vertical gap between the RD and TD curves is widest near true strain ~0.3 and narrows towards the highest strains, where RD approaches 10 ×10^14 m⁻² while TD stays near 9 ×10^14 m⁻².

The caption states panel (a) shows the ΔK−βW_hkl versus KC^1/2 relation determined by the modified Williamson-Hall method for five FCC reflections {111}, {200}, {220}, {311}, {222} in both RD and TD samples at two strain levels, and panel (b) shows austenite dislocation density versus true strain for the two samples.

The citing text states the dislocation density was obtained from the slope of the (ΔK−βW_hkl)–KC^1/2 relation, with the RD samples exhibiting higher slopes than the TD sample and therefore a higher dislocation density.
The citing text states that β was determined by trial-and-error so that ΔK−βW_hkl follows a smooth quadratic curve according to Eq. (3), giving β = 0.002 (RD) and 0.004 (TD) at true strain ~0.14.
The citing text states the austenite dislocation density of the RD sample is higher than that of TD by a maximum value of ~1.51 × 10^14 m⁻².
The citing text states that the dislocation density of the BCC (ferrite/martensite) phase was not analysed because its diffraction peaks are highly overlapped and difficult to separate.

The citing text attributes the higher austenite dislocation density of the RD sample to strain-induced α'-martensitic transformation, via transformation-induced local plasticity and stress/strain partitioning, and notes that the RD–TD difference decreases above 0.35 true strain, possibly due to martensite transformation of highly dislocated austenite, so dislocation multiplication differences should not explain the different strain-hardening ability.

subfigures.description: Modified Williamson-Hall plot at ε=0.14: y = ΔK−βW_hkl (0.00–0.10 nm⁻¹) vs x = KC^1/2 (1.5–5.0 nm⁻¹), with β_RD=0.002 and β_TD=0.004 printed in the upper-left. Five points per sample labelled 111, 200, 220, 311, 222 (filled squares = RD, open squares = TD); red RD and blue TD linear fits nearly overlap, separating only slightly at low KC^1/2.

Same modified Williamson-Hall axes at ε=0.22, with β_RD=0.0018 and β_TD=0.0044 printed in the upper-left. Five RD points (filled circles, red) and five TD points (open circles, blue) labelled 111, 200, 220, 311, 222; the red RD line lies clearly above the blue TD line at every reflection, giving a visibly steeper slope for RD.

Scatter plot of austenite dislocation density (×10^14 m⁻², axis 0–10) against true strain (0.0–0.5), with two open-circle curves labelled RD (red) and TD (blue). Both increase monotonically with strain; the two curves are indistinguishable and cross at very low strain (<~0.05), after which RD stays above TD, the separation being largest around 0.3 strain and narrowing towards the highest strains (~0.45) where RD approaches 10 ×10^14 m⁻².

unreadable_items: In panel (a) the red and blue index labels 200/220/311 cluster tightly between KC^1/2 ≈ 3.0 and 3.8 at both strain levels, so which marker belongs to which individual reflection is only partly separable
